We are given that [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are parallel. Since line [MATH: t] intersects both lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n,] it is a transversal.

The angle labeled [MATH: 60^\circ] and the angle labeled [MATH: x^\circ] are consecutive interior angles because they are on the same side of the transversal [MATH: t] and between the parallel lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n.]

When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, consecutive interior angles are supplementary. So, we can write

[MATH: x^\circ + 60^\circ = 180^\circ.]

Solving for [MATH: x,] we get

[MATH: x^\circ = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ.]

Therefore, we can conclude that [MATH: x = 120.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Questions about consecutive angles often appear in geometry problems involving parallel lines, polygons, and transversals, where recognizing supplementary relationships quickly can save time.

Content:
By practicing these patterns until they become second nature, we’ll strengthen our geometric reasoning and improve test efficiency.

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Consecutive Interior Angles

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/9eaf476a2a026ea6aed8c92189c9587a]

In the diagram above, lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are parallel, and the line [MATH: t] intersects both. What is the value of [MATH: x?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are given that [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are parallel. Since line [MATH: t] intersects both lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n,] it is a transversal.

The angle labeled [MATH: 60^\circ] and the angle labeled [MATH: x^\circ] are consecutive interior angles because they are on the same side of the transversal [MATH: t] and between the parallel lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n.]

When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, consecutive interior angles are supplementary. So, we can write

[MATH: x^\circ + 60^\circ = 180^\circ.]

Solving for [MATH: x,] we get

[MATH: x^\circ = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ.]

Therefore, we can conclude that [MATH: x = 120.]
